evidence.item: Scenario F: NoPartialFillExchange vs PartialFillExchange genuinely diverge (oversized single order)
evidence.setup: IOC buy for 150 shares against a touch quoting only 100 shares at 10.02.

actual_result.no_partial_fill: FILLED in full: exec_qty=150.0, status=FILLED. Fills the ENTIRE requested quantity unconditionally on any cross, never checking quoted size -- documented upstream: 'this may cause unrealistic fill simulations if you attempt to execute a large quantity' (nopartialfillexchange.rs struct doc, ~lines 58-62).
actual_result.partial_fill: EXPIRED, but exec_qty=100.0 (not 0), leaves_qty=50.0. Walks quoted depth, executes what is available (100), then overwrites status to Expired even though a partial fill already executed and updated state.

evidence.status_understates_caveat_scope: This 'status alone understates what happened' caveat is IOC-SPECIFIC. Scenario G2 (FOK, insufficient depth, PartialFillExchange) correctly expires with exec_qty EXACTLY 0 -- FOK computes cumulative available quantity BEFORE executing anything and only proceeds if it is sufficient, so there is nothing partial to understate. An earlier version of this receipt did not scope this caveat to IOC.
evidence.conclusion: The two exchange models are NOT equivalent in general. They coincided on Scenarios A-D and G1/G3/G4 only because those fixtures kept order size at or below the touch's quoted size -- and even that coincidence set excludes G2, which diverges.

evidence.item: Scenario I: PartialFillExchange's own no-depletion bias (NEW this round)
evidence.reviewer_probe: Three back-to-back 100-share IOCs against a touch that always shows exactly 100 shares (never re-quoted, for the whole 10s run).
evidence.upstream_citation: partialfillexchange.rs struct doc comment, ~lines 66-69 (verified by reading the pinned source): 'Liquidity-taking orders will be executed based on the quantity of the order book, EVEN THOUGH THE BEST PRICE AND QUANTITY DO NOT CHANGE DUE TO YOUR EXECUTION. Be aware that this may cause unrealistic fill simulations if you attempt to execute a large quantity.'
evidence.conclusion: PartialFillExchange caps a SINGLE order's fill at the displayed size, but never actually depletes that display for the NEXT order -- so at a high enough submission rate it over-fills, structurally similar to Scenario F/G2's single-oversized-order case but spread across multiple orders. Calling PartialFillExchange 'realistic' (an earlier version of this receipt implied this by contrast with NoPartialFillExchange, without qualification) overstates it; this bias is now listed next to Scenario E in the verdict.

evidence.item: EMO at-quote rule and Lee-Ready rule, offered separately -- exact-quote condition corrected, citation corrected
evidence.constructed_by: this task, blueprints/us-equities/sim-crosscheck-hftbacktest/l1_feasibility.py (infer_side_emo, infer_side_lee_ready, _tick_test, run_scenario_c_emo, run_scenario_d1_with_inferred_side, run_tick_test_coverage_demo, run_emo_boundary_demo)
evidence.citation_correction: Verified directly against the NBER page's own metadata (citation_author, citation_title meta tags): NBER Working Paper No. 14158 is 'Short Sales and Trade Classification Algorithms' by Paul Asquith, Rebecca Oman, and Christopher Safaya (2008), a study measuring how often EMO/Lee-Ready/tick-test misclassify SHORT SALES specifically -- not a general literature review, and not authored by 'Diether, Lee & Werner' as an earlier version of this receipt claimed without checking.
evidence.exact_quote_correction: An earlier version of infer_side_emo used `trade_px >= ask` / `trade_px <= bid` (at-or-through the quote). EMO's own at-quote condition is EQUALITY: now `trade_px == ask` / `trade_px == bid`, with everything else -- including strictly-inside-the-spread prints AND prints outside the quotes entirely (above the ask or below the bid) -- falling to the tick test. run_emo_boundary_demo() (prices [10.00, 10.02, 10.03, 9.98]) confirms: exactly-at-bid -> direct sell; exactly-at-ask -> direct buy; strictly-above-ask (10.03) -> tick test (an uptick from the ask, happens to also resolve 'buy', but via the fallback, not the at-quote condition); strictly-below-bid (9.98) -> tick test (a downtick, resolves 'sell'). Directly confirmed with no prior trade history at all, infer_side_emo(10.05,...) and infer_side_emo(9.90,...) both return None (undetermined) -- proof the at-quote condition itself is not what classified the boundary-demo prints.
evidence.existing_disagreement_tape_unaffected: TICK_TEST_TRIGGER_PRICES's EMO-vs-Lee-Ready disagreement (index 1, price 10.015) is UNCHANGED by the exact-quote fix: that print was always strictly inside the spread, never at either quote, so it always used the tick test under both the old and new EMO implementations.

d1_inferred_side_actually_run.correction_of: An earlier version of this receipt claimed inference 'restores trade-through fills in this fixture' on the D1 tape WITHOUT ever running it.
d1_inferred_side_actually_run.setup: The D1 print (9.99) is OUTSIDE the quotes (below the bid, not at it, bid=10.00/ask=10.02), so a bare single-trade tape gives EMO no prior price for the tick test (returns None/undetermined). run_scenario_d1_with_inferred_side() adds one unambiguous seed trade at the ask (400ms) before the 9.99 print (500ms), giving the tick test a genuine prior price.
d1_inferred_side_actually_run.actual_result: inferred_sides = ['buy' (seed, direct at-quote), 'sell' (9.99, tick test: downtick from 10.02)]. Applying these inferred bits: FILLED, exec_qty=5.0 -- inference DOES restore the trade-through fill, now genuinely verified rather than assumed.

evidence.scenario_c_emo_result: Applying EMO to Scenario C's original trade tape (all 5 prints exactly at the bid) classifies every one as a sell aggressor -- FILLED, exec_qty=5.0, matching with_side=True.
evidence.claim_boundary: This is OUR proposed data-preparation step, not an hftbacktest feature. Only demonstrated on hand-constructed synthetic tapes, not on real Alpaca SIP data.

feasible_for: Order acceptance and marketable-crossing fills driven by top-of-book depth alone (Scenarios A, D3)

IOC/FOK/GTX time-in-force semantics for G1/G3/G4 (sufficient-depth FOK, crossing GTX -> Expired never Rejected, non-crossing GTX rests like GTC) -- G2 (oversized FOK) diverges between exchange models, see below
Constant order latency (entry + response), independent of depth granularity (Scenarios A/B)
TradingValueFeeModel cost accounting on realized fills, verified with a nonzero taker fee (Scenario H)
Both exchange models for depth-crossing fill/expiry paths on Scenarios A-D and G1/G3/G4's specific order sizes -- NOT a general equivalence
not_feasible_or_meaningless_for: Any trade-driven fill path without an aggressor side (Scenarios C, D1) -- neither exchange model reaches the trade-driven code path at all for a side-less TRADE_EVENT.

Distinguishing NoPartialFillExchange from PartialFillExchange in general: they diverge on order-exceeds-touch-size (Scenario F), FOK-with-insufficient-depth (Scenario G2), AND on repeated orders against a constant-size touch (Scenario I, new) -- a cross-check plan must pick one deliberately and account for its specific gap, not treat 'PartialFillExchange' as simply 'the realistic one'.

PartialFillExchange as a stand-in for genuine liquidity consumption across orders: it never depletes `self.depth` from a fill at all (Scenario I) -- three 100-share IOCs against an always-100 touch all fill in full, position 300.

Trusting a resting order's queue position as realistic when accepted at a price the L1 feed had never quoted: zero queue-ahead, producing an optimistic fill-speed bias (Scenario E, now HAND-VERIFIED, not merely measured).
The L3 FIFO queue model (needs per-order add/cancel/execute events); categorically unavailable from L1 or standard L2 SIP quotes.
Any depth-percentile / multi-level queue heuristic reading levels beyond the touch.
l1_feasibility_verdict.mitigation: An EMO or Lee-Ready aggressor-side inference step, applied as data preparation, restores trade-driven queue depletion AND trade-through fills (Scenario D1, now actually run with a seed trade) -- at the cost of classification error not quantified here on real data. Scenario E's queue-position optimism and Scenario I's no-depletion bias have no mitigation identified; they are inherent properties of hftbacktest's exchange models as applied to L1 data at a submission rate exceeding what the displayed size alone would support.
not_exercised: IntpOrderLatency (interpolated, recorded-data-driven latency) and per-symbol latency variation.
FlatPerTradeFeeModel and TradingQtyFeeModel -- only TradingValueFeeModel was exercised (Scenario H).

L3FIFOQueueModel and RiskAdverseQueueModel (a conservative queue-position estimator, per upstream's own naming) -- only ProbQueueModel was exercised. Scenario E's bias almost certainly generalizes to RiskAdverseQueueModel too (identical zero-queue-ahead-on-a-fresh-price new_order() behavior, queue.rs ~lines 67-74), not separately measured.
l1_feasibility_verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading hftbacktest/src/backtest/proc/{nopartialfillexchange,partialfillexchange}.rs and hftbacktest/src/backtest/models/queue.rs line-by-line for every code path this fixture exercises, then reproducing each path with a hand-verified fixture where tractable (Scenarios A-D, E, G, D1-inferred-side) and an explicitly labeled observed run where not (none remain unlabeled as of this round).

nautilus_taker_queue_claim_corrected.corrected_claim: For IOC/marketable takers, NautilusTrader's queue-position mechanism (snapshot_queue_position) is simply never invoked at all -- it is not a matter of Nautilus assuming a different queue state, there IS no queue state involved for a taker fill in either engine, for related but distinct reasons (Nautilus: no notion of queue position applies to an immediate fill at all; hftbacktest: queue position applies only to RESTING orders, and a taker order by definition doesn't rest).
